title: Episode 331: Edward VIII & George VI: The Abdication of 1936, the King's Speech, and the Blitz
description:
The monumental constitutional trauma of the 1936 Abdication and the wartime redemption of the British crown. King Edward VIII, the glamorous, adored Prince of Wales, threw the British Empire into constitutional turmoil when he chose love over duty, renouncing the throne after just 326 days to marry the twice-divorced American socialite Wallis Simpson. Thrust onto the throne was his shy, stammering younger brother Albert, who took the regnal name George VI. Overcoming his severe speech impediment with the aid of speech therapist Lionel Logue, George VI and Queen Elizabeth stood resolutely with Londoners through the terrifying nights of the Blitz, visiting the bombed East End and refusing to evacuate their children. Discover how a stammering, reluctant king saved the British monarchy and rallied a beleaguered nation to victory in World War II.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Kings and Queens of England series covers the defining constitutional crisis and greatest moral trial of the modern era: the 1936 Abdication of Edward VIII and the heroic wartime reign of his brother, King George VI. Here is George with the extraordinary story of the stammering king who united an empire in its darkest hour.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE GOLDEN PRINCE AND THE ABDICATION CRISIS: 1894 TO DECEMBER 1936
Born in June 1894 at White Lodge, Richmond, Edward Albert Christian George Andrew Patrick David—known affectionately as David to his family—was the premier royal superstar of the twentieth century. Dashing, blond, athletic, and effortlessly modern, the young Prince of Wales had toured the globe in the 1920s, captivating crowds from Canada and Australia to India and the United States with his magnetic charm, youthful fashion, and empathetic common touch. Yet beneath the glamorous facade, David chafed violently against the rigid strictures of court protocol and constitutional duty, confiding to his intimates that he felt imprisoned by the crown. In 1931, David met Wallis Warfield Simpson, a sharp-witted, sophisticated American woman from Baltimore who was then married to her second husband, shipping executive Ernest Simpson. Edward became hopelessly infatuated with Wallis, finding in her dominant, assertive personality an emotional shelter he had never known in his austere royal childhood. When King George V died in January 1936, David ascended the throne as King Edward VIII. Within months, it became glaringly evident that the King intended to marry Wallis as soon as her pending divorce was finalized. Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin and the governments of the self-governing Commonwealth Dominions delivered a blunt, uncompromising ultimatum: as Supreme Governor of the Church of England—which then strictly forbade the remarriage of divorced persons whose former spouses were living—Edward could not marry Wallis and remain king. On December 10, 1936, Edward chose love over duty, signing the historic Instrument of Abdication after a reign of only three hundred and twenty-six days. The following night, broadcasting to a stunned empire from Windsor Castle, the uncrowned king spoke the immortal words: 'I have found it impossible to carry the heavy burden of responsibility and to discharge my duties as king as I would wish to do, without the help and support of the woman I love.' Created Duke of Windsor, he departed into lifelong continental exile.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE KING'S SPEECH: BERTIE AND LIONEL LOGUE: 1926 TO 1937
The abdication struck Edward's younger brother, Prince Albert, Duke of York—known to his family as Bertie—like a catastrophic thunderbolt. Quiet, profoundly sensitive, and plagued from early childhood with chronic digestive illnesses and knock-knees that required painful leg splints, Bertie had lived in terror of the royal limelight. Above all, he suffered from a severe, agonizing stammer that paralyzed his vocal cords in public, making speeches a torturous ordeal of long, agonizing silences and physical strain. In October 1925, Bertie's disastrous closing speech at the British Empire Exhibition at Wembley Stadium had left him humiliated and near tears. Desperate for help, Bertie's devoted wife, Lady Elizabeth Bowes-Lyon, brought him to the consulting rooms of Lionel Logue, an unorthodox, self-taught Australian speech therapist practicing in Harley Street. Logue treated the royal prince not with formal deference, but as an equal, prescribing physical breathing exercises, tongue twisters, diaphragmatic relaxation, and deep psychological reassurance, addressing the root causes of Bertie's childhood trauma and fear. When the abdication crisis suddenly forced the crown upon Bertie's reluctant brow in December 1936, the Duke wept openly on his mother Queen Mary's shoulder for an hour. Taking the regnal name George VI to emphasize continuity with his father's steady, respectable reign, Bertie faced his coronation at Westminster Abbey on May 12, 1937. With Lionel Logue watching anxiously from the royal box, the new King spoke his solemn coronation oaths with clear, unwavering dignity, transforming personal terror into quiet, inspirational majesty.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE GATHERING STORM AND MUNICH: 1937 TO 1939
King George VI and Queen Elizabeth assumed the crown in a world rushing headlong toward catastrophe. In Germany, Adolf Hitler had dismantled the Treaty of Versailles, militarized the Rhineland, and annexed Austria, while Benito Mussolini's fascist Italy rampaged across Ethiopia. Dedicated to preserving peace for their war-weary people, the King and Queen initially supported Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain's policy of European appeasement. When Chamberlain returned from Munich in September 1938 waving his infamous 'Piece of Paper' promising peace in our time, George VI took the highly unusual constitutional step of inviting Chamberlain to appear beside the royal family on the balcony of Buckingham Palace to receive the cheers of the ecstatic crowd. Yet the King harbored deep private misgivings about Nazi aggression, quietly urging the rapid rearmament of the Royal Air Force and Royal Navy. In May and June 1939, George VI and Queen Elizabeth embarked on a triumphant, historic state visit to Canada and the United States, becoming the first reigning British monarch to cross the Atlantic and visit Washington. Hosted by President Franklin D. Roosevelt at the White House and at Hyde Park—where the royal couple famously dined on hot dogs at an informal picnic—the King's quiet sincerity and the Queen's radiant charm forged an indispensable bond of Anglo-American solidarity that would prove decisive in the existential struggle ahead.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE KING AND QUEEN IN THE BLITZ: 1940 TO 1941
When Great Britain declared war on Nazi Germany on September 3, 1939, King George VI broadcast to the worldwide British Empire from Buckingham Palace, delivering a somber, magnificent radio address that rallied millions of souls: 'In this grave hour, perhaps the most memorable in our history, I send to every household of my peoples... this message, spoken with the same depth of feeling for each one of you as if I were able to cross your threshold and speak to you myself.' With Lionel Logue standing just feet away, directing the King's breathing with quiet hand gestures, George spoke with measured, resonant authority. In May 1940, as France collapsed and Winston Churchill became Prime Minister, the King initially viewed the pugnacious statesman with suspicion, but the two men quickly developed an intimate, affectionate wartime partnership, meeting every Tuesday for private, unminuted lunches. When the Luftwaffe launched the Blitz in September 1940, raining fire and high explosives upon London for fifty-seven consecutive nights, the royal family flatly refused government advice to evacuate to the safety of Canada. Queen Elizabeth declared defiantly: 'The children won't go without me. I won't leave the King. And the King will never leave.' On September 13, 1940, a German bomber dropped six five-hundred-pound bombs directly onto Buckingham Palace, destroying the royal chapel and shattering windows just yards from where the King and Queen stood. Inspecting the smoldering ruins, Queen Elizabeth made the immortal remark: 'I'm glad we've been bombed. It makes me feel I can look the East End in the face.' Daily, the royal couple toured the devastated streets of London, Coventry, and Birmingham, climbing over smoking rubble to comfort grieving families.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE ROYAL FAMILY AT WAR: WINDSOR, NORMANDY, AND VE DAY: 1942 TO 1945
Throughout the grueling years of total war, King George VI shared every sacrifice endured by his civilian subjects. At Buckingham Palace and Windsor Castle, hot bathwater was strictly rationed to a depth of five inches, marked by a painted black line inside the royal bathtubs, while the King and Queen held official ration books and dined on coarse wartime Spam, turnip stews, and powdered eggs. The King practiced pistol shooting in the palace gardens, determined to sell his life dearly if German paratroopers attacked London. In 1942, personal tragedy struck the royal family when the King's dashing younger brother, Prince George, Duke of Kent, was killed in an active service plane crash in Scotland. In 1943, George VI flew under heavy escort to North Africa and Malta, presenting the island fortress with the George Cross—a civilian medal of gallantry he had personally instituted in 1940 to honor courageous civilians. In June 1944, just ten days after D-Day, the King sailed across the English Channel to Normandy aboard HMS Arethusa, landing on Juno Beach under artillery fire to decorate General Bernard Montgomery and greet his frontline troops. When victory in Europe finally arrived on May 8, 1945, wild, jubilant crowds swarmed the gates of Buckingham Palace. The King, Queen, and their daughters, Princesses Elizabeth and Margaret, appeared eight times on the palace balcony beside Winston Churchill, greeted by an ocean of roaring citizens who recognized that the quiet, dutiful monarch had been the beating moral heart of the Allied victory.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: POSTWAR AUSTERITY, THE NHS, AND THE FESTIVAL OF BRITAIN: 1945 TO 1951
Victory left Great Britain militarily triumphant but financially bankrupted and physically exhausted. In the July 1945 general election, the British electorate decisively voted out Churchill and swept Clement Attlee's Labour Party into power with a landslide mandate for sweeping social revolution. King George VI handled the radical political transition with flawless constitutional impartiality. He established an excellent, cooperative relationship with Attlee, supporting the historic creation of the National Health Service in 1948, the nationalization of key industries, and the founding of the modern British welfare state. Abroad, the British Empire underwent a profound, rapid metamorphosis: in 1947, India and Pakistan achieved independence, and George VI surrendered his title as Emperor of India, embracing the revolutionary concept of the modern Commonwealth—a voluntary association of free and equal sovereign nations recognizing the British monarch as the symbolic Head of the Commonwealth. In 1951, seeking to lift the spirits of a weary people enduring strict postwar rationing and grim austerity, the King opened the Festival of Britain on London's South Bank, a dazzling celebration of British art, architecture, and scientific genius that pointed the way toward a brighter, modern future.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE FINAL WAVE AT LONDON AIRPORT AND THE KING'S PASSING: FEBRUARY 1952
The relentless physical strain of the war and postwar crises, combined with lifelong heavy cigarette smoking, took a catastrophic toll on King George VI's health. Suffering from severe arteriosclerosis, Buerger's disease, and lung cancer, the King underwent grueling surgery in September 1951 to remove his entire left lung. Though desperately frail and pale, his sense of royal duty never wavered. On January 31, 1952, despite bitter freezing winds and doctors' stern warnings, the King traveled to London Airport to bid farewell to his twenty-five-year-old daughter Princess Elizabeth and the Duke of Edinburgh as they embarked on a six-month Commonwealth tour. Standing bareheaded on the tarmac, his hair whipped by the icy gale, the haggard King waved a long, poignant farewell to the plane carrying his beloved daughter—a moving image captured by press photographers that became the nation's final memory of their courageous sovereign. Six days later, on the night of February 5, 1952, after a happy day of shooting hares on the Sandringham estate, King George VI retired to bed and died peacefully in his sleep from a coronary thrombosis at the age of fifty-six. A grief-stricken nation and an empire mourned a monarch who had never sought the crown, yet had worn it with unequaled nobility, restoring faith in the British monarchy and leaving an immortal legacy of duty, sacrifice, and quiet courage.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
King George VI was laid to rest at St. George's Chapel, Windsor, remembered forever as the quiet man who conquered his infirmities to lead his nation through its darkest hour. Join us next time as we begin the record-breaking reign of his daughter, Queen Elizabeth II, from her accession in the African wilderness to the crowning splendor of the 1953 coronation. Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
